01-lightning.answer: Lightning moves Bitcoin through 2-of-2 payment channels so transactions never touch the chain until you close. Tyler walks through how a channel works, HTLCs, inbound liquidity, always-on nodes, and why the math says it can't onboard 7 billion people.
chapters: Intro
What Lightning is and why it exists
How a channel works: the 2-of-2 pot and HTLCs
The downsides: inbound liquidity, nodes, locked capital
tags: how does the lightning network work

02-quantum.answer: Short answer: not today, and the real exposure is address reuse, not the curve. Tyler explains Q-Day vs a classical break, why Ethereum reuses addresses by default, Justin Drake's bunker-mode advice, and what a cleartext internet would look like.
chapters: Intro
The OpenAI math paper and the 'AI breaks Bitcoin' headline
Justin Drake says go bunker mode
Q-Day vs a classical break, address reuse
How you'd disclose a broken curve
The internet goes back to cleartext

03-bitcoin-l2.answer: A Bitcoin L2 is anything that lets you move Bitcoin off-chain and still exit back to L1 without anyone's permission. Tyler defines the term, applies the unilateral-exit test to Arbitrum, and compares Lightning, Spark and Ark.
chapters: Intro
What a Bitcoin layer two actually is
Is Arbitrum still an L2? The unilateral-exit test
Ark vs Spark
What Spark's exit really costs

04-spark.answer: Spark is a Bitcoin L2 from Lightspark that drops Lightning's channels for a federation of operators. Tyler explains how it works, the unilateral-exit story (22 leaves, 253 transactions, 80% of the wallet gone in fees), and why operators see every transaction.
chapters: Intro
What Spark is and who built it
How Spark works: the federation and service providers
Unilateral exit and what it costs
Privacy: operators see everything

05-coldcard.answer: A Coldcard firmware bug shipped weak entropy for five years and an AI agent found it. Tyler explains what went wrong, who was spared, why he rolls dice 100 times for his own seed, and whether self-custody is cooked.
chapters: Intro
The Coldcard catastrophe
Dice rolls and who was spared
Is self-custody cooked?

06-liquid.answer: White hats drained roughly $300M from Blockstream's Liquid sidechain, kept a fee, and the federation wants the rest back. Tyler explains what a federated sidechain is, the proof-check bug, the white hat fee, and the update two weeks later.
chapters: Intro
White hats drained Liquid: how a federated sidechain works
The white hat fee, the FBI, North Korea or a teenager
Update: Blockstream wants the last 15% back

07-anonymous.answer: Bitcoin is pseudonymous, not anonymous, and a handful of multi-billion-dollar surveillance firms make sure of it. Jackson (ex-fraud) on why hiding is fruitless, Tyler's actual opsec, shielded Bitcoin, Ark, and honeypot nodes.
chapters: Intro
Why trying to be anonymous is fruitless
Tyler's opsec: Tor, Tails, a cash laptop
Is shielded Bitcoin legit?
Ark already gives privacy off-chain
Chain surveillance firms and honeypot nodes

08-mev.answer: MEV is the money validators and bots extract by reordering transactions. Chris explains how a $15M sandwich bot got sandwiched with a fake wrapped token, then why Jito's grip on Solana staking makes MEV a cash flow, not a crime.
chapters: Intro
The $15M sandwich bot that got sandwiched
Jito: the MEV monopoly on Solana

09-hardware-wallet.answer: $102M in Bitcoin left Ledger wallets through a physical implant with a SIM card, not a software bug. Tyler and Chris on how the supply chain got hit, whether self-custody is dead, and the fixes: multi-vendor multisig and Bitcoin vaults.
chapters: Intro
The Ledger implant: what happened
Is self-custody dead?
Chris wants to build a hardware wallet
Fixes: multi-vendor multisig and vaults

10-enclaves.answer: A secure enclave runs code where even the host can't look, and an attestation proves which code. Chris explains TEEs and attestation, why it only works with open source or a trusted auditor, and what it means when an AI agent buys your shoes.
chapters: Intro
Muse and secure enclaves
What an attestation actually proves
LLMs and infinite surveillance
The payments story: Stripe Link and Meta as aggregator
I let Facebook buy my shoes

11-stablecoin-issuers.answer: Stablecoin issuers make money on the float, and a bank found the glitch: buy USDT at 99.99 cents, redeem at a dollar, forever. Chris explains the trade, then (from Ep 4) the burn desk, the exit every issuer controls.
chapters: Intro
The infinite money glitch: buy at 99.99, redeem at 1.00
The burn desk: how issuers control the exit

12-agi-levels.answer: DeepMind's framework has five levels of AGI, and by its definition ChatGPT was already 'emerging AGI' in 2023. Jackson and Chris walk the table, argue where today's models sit, and whether 'can it make me money' is the real test.
chapters: Intro
Sam Altman says AGI by end of 2026
DeepMind's five levels
Where ChatGPT and today's models sit
